clue.text: Bewilder fellows looking into party’s U-turn at start of election

indicators.note: to look into something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within another
a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters run in the opposite direction
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: Lab is short for the Labour Party
F is the abbreviation for fellow, doubled for the plural
first letter of election

explanation.surface: Voters are baffled when a party abandons its policies just as an election begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' here is Labour, shortened as crosswords often do; the fellows sit inside the reversed party, not inside the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: To baffle someone is to confuse or perplex them completely, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Bum team’s after a defender

indicators.note: one thing coming after another sets their order in the answer, the later piece placed second

blocks.note: a back is a defending player in football or rugby
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that a useless team is chasing a single defender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as an adjective meaning worthless, but it is the noun for the buttocks; 'team's' is 'team is', the side that comes after.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a bum is the buttocks, the part of the body you sit on, also called the backside.

clue.text: Unrealistic when stubbornly keeping social worker in charge

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: to hold fast is to cling stubbornly
the ant is the classic social insect worker
IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Someone stubbornly holding on to a social worker who runs things is being unrealistic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a care professional, but crosswords use it for an insect from a colony; holding fast is clinging stubbornly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic in its older sense means fanciful or imaginary, far removed from reality.

clue.text: Enticement of riches about to disappear

indicators.note: something that disappears is no longer there, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: lucre is money or wealth, as in filthy lucre
C stands for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: The temptation of wealth that is about to vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to disappear' reads as 'soon to vanish', but it means the abbreviation for about, C, disappears from LUCRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lure is a bait or temptation that draws someone in, the same idea as an enticement.

clue.text: Assured by potential displayed at the outset

indicators.note: the outset is the very beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a young player showing promise has potential
first letter of displayed

explanation.surface: Someone reassured by the talent a newcomer showed early on.
explanation.walkthrough: The D goes at the end even though 'displayed' comes after 'potential' only by chance; the charade simply reads in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To have promised something is to have assured someone it will happen, giving a firm guarantee.

clue.text: About to find grudge causing temporary delay

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
spite is malice or a grudge against someone

explanation.surface: Someone close to discovering a grudge that holds things up for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'About' alone is the short word for concerning and 'to find' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A respite is a short pause or postponement, especially a stay of punishment or a break from hardship.

clue.text: It’s used in measurement of time miller wasted

indicators.note: something wasted is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are knocked out of their order

blocks.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint about how a miller fritters away hours when time is being measured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measurement of time' looks like the definition, a clock or watch, but the definition stops at 'measurement'; 'time miller' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A millimetre is a metric unit of length, one thousandth of a metre, used whenever small distances are recorded.

clue.text: England’s opener coming after Pole’s save

indicators.note: an opener comes first, so only the initial letter is taken
coming after another thing puts this piece second in the sequence

blocks.note: a spar is a pole, as used for a ship's mast or boom
first letter of England

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: England's opening batsman follows a Polish keeper's save.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' is capitalised to suggest a Polish person, but it is a plain pole, a SPAR; the possessive 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To spare something is to save it, either by not using it or by keeping it from harm.

clue.text: Close to breaking engagement present

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: on can mean next to or close to, as in a town on the coast
a date is a social engagement or appointment

explanation.surface: An engagement on the verge of breaking off, with a present involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a betrothal near collapse; instead 'engagement' is a DATE and 'Close to' is ON, which breaks into it.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to give it formally, and to donate is to give it as a gift, so both are verbs.

clue.text: Hardy character ultimately having nothing, facing police arrest

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: last letter of character
O looks like zero, nothing
a bust is a police raid or arrest

explanation.surface: A Thomas Hardy character, penniless in the end, facing arrest by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' reads as the novelist Thomas Hardy, but it is the adjective meaning tough.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hardy can endure harsh conditions, and robust means strong and resilient in the same way.

clue.text: Tory complaint largely about Unite’s leader being in agreement

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not wholly, so the last letter is dropped
a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is used
about means around, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: Con is short for Conservative
a grouse is a grumble or complaint
first letter of Unite

explanation.surface: A Conservative grumbles about the trade union Unite's boss, yet the two end up agreeing.
explanation.walkthrough: GROUSE loses its last letter to give GROUS, which goes around the U; Unite is a large British trade union, so the surface pits a Tory against its leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Congruous describes things that fit together or correspond, so they are in harmony or accord.

clue.text: Find out from part of cochlear nerve

indicators.note: a part of something is a piece of it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Discovering something from a section of the nerve that carries hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the end of cochLEAR into the N of Nerve; the cochlear nerve links the inner ear to the brain.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn a fact is to discover or find it out, a common verb synonym.

clue.text: Rule of law eventually stopping for example

indicators.note: eventually means in the end, so only the last letter is used
to stop a hole is to plug it, so one piece fills the middle of another

blocks.note: last letter of law
say introduces an example, like for example

explanation.surface: The rule of law, which in the end stops crime, offered as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule of law' reads as a single phrase, but the definition is just 'Rule' and 'of' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold sway is to have power or control, so sway as a noun means dominion or rule.

clue.text: Generous of Miles to find tunic fine after repair

indicators.note: after a repair things are put back together in a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for miles
the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Praise for a man called Miles, who finds a tunic looking good once mended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miles' poses as a man's name but is only the abbreviation M.
explanation.definitionFit: Munificent means lavishly giving, so it describes a person who is very open-handed and liberal.

clue.text: What record producers do to get leave

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: producers create the songs on an album
second meaning: an idiom for setting off or departing

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what music producers do in order to be granted time off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get leave' sounds like being given a holiday, but 'leave' is a verb here, the idiom for heading off.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial idiom for departing quickly, and literally describes recording individual songs on an album.

clue.text: Diminish the value of French painting back at court

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite order

blocks.note: de is French for of
painting is a form of art
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Talk of how a French painting hanging at court has lost its worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of French' reads as describing the painting, but it means the French word for of.
explanation.definitionFit: To detract from something is to take away from its worth, lessening its merit or quality.

clue.text: Eleven Socceroos embracing nevertheless

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within your arms, so the words hold the letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A football team of eleven Australians hugging each other regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: The Socceroos are Australia's national football team; the answer sits inside elEVEN SOcceroos.
explanation.definitionFit: Even so is an adverbial phrase meaning however or in spite of that, the same sense as nevertheless.

clue.text: Conference room finally found after bit of searching by my pious doctor

indicators.note: a bit is a small piece, here the opening letter only
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered in order
finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept
coming after places this piece later in the sequence than the rest

blocks.note: first letter of searching
the seven letters taken as written
last letter of room

explanation.surface: A devout doctor of mine searches and at last finds the conference room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conference room' reads as one place, but the definition is 'Conference' alone; 'doctor' is a verb here, not the pious physician.
explanation.definitionFit: A symposium is a meeting where experts gather to discuss a subject, a kind of academic gathering.

clue.text: Swimmer describing more sick banter

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw it round something, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: a ray is a flat fish, a swimmer
iller is the comparative of ill

explanation.surface: An athlete in the pool talking about even more tasteless jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' looks like 'talking about', but it is the geometric sense, tracing a line round something.
explanation.definitionFit: Raillery is good-humoured teasing or ridicule, which is what banter amounts to.

clue.text: Stress caused by Bill needing money perhaps

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
a cent is an example of money

explanation.surface: A man called Bill, short of cash, is worried sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' poses as a man's name but is an invoice, abbreviated AC; 'perhaps' marks the cent as one example of money.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent is the emphasis placed on a syllable, so it is the same as stress in speech.

clue.text: Sport in which number one is red Ted? Gosh, amazing

definitions.text: Sport in which number one is red

indicators.note: to amaze once meant to bewilder or stupefy, so the letters are thrown into confusion

blocks.note: the seven letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in wonder that in some sport the top player is a red-faced Ted.
explanation.walkthrough: In greyhound racing the dog in trap one always wears a red jacket; 'the dogs' is the British name for an evening at the greyhound track.
explanation.definitionFit: Greyhound racing, called the dogs in Britain, assigns jacket colours by trap, and trap one is red.

clue.text: Girl packing doctor’s musical instrument

indicators.note: to pack something is to stow it inside, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: Maria is a girl's name
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A girl puts a doctor's musical instrument into her bag.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'doctor's' is just 'is', linking the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A marimba is a percussion instrument like a large xylophone, with wooden bars over resonators.

clue.text: Complain of my original total

indicators.note: the original is what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: first letter of my
utter means total or complete, as in utter chaos

explanation.surface: Someone grumbling about their original sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total' reads as a noun, a sum, but it is the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: To mutter is to grumble under your breath, a muted way of expressing discontent.

clue.text: Well-known local runner article ignored

indicators.note: something ignored is left out of account, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, and the person who runs it is the publican
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A familiar figure in the area, a runner who ignored an article about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local runner' suggests an athlete from the area; in British usage your local is your nearest pub, and its runner is the publican.
explanation.definitionFit: Something public is openly known to everyone, as in public knowledge, so it is widely recognised.

clue.text: Name tune heard curiously coming from below

indicators.note: done curiously means done in an odd way, so the letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
the nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone names a tune they heard oddly drifting up from downstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name tune' sounds like a quiz instruction, but 'Name' gives only N, joining the letters of 'tune heard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Underneath means directly beneath or lower down, a straightforward synonym for below.

clue.text: The inversion of Mercury, for instance, is supported by academic in principle

indicators.note: inverting turns something upside down, which in a down clue runs the letters the other way
in a down clue what is supported sits on top, so the support comes underneath and later

blocks.note: Mercury is the Roman messenger god
MA, Master of Arts, stands for an academic

explanation.surface: An academic, in principle, backs a theory about mercury turning upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mercury' suggests the metal or the planet; 'for instance' marks it as an example of a god.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogma is a fixed belief or tenet laid down as true, a principle held without question.

clue.text: Half-hearted dupe swallowing piece of unagi? Disgusting

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two central letters is removed
a piece is a small part, here only the opening letter
to swallow is to take inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: to dupe someone is to fool them, and a dupe is a fool
first letter of unagi

explanation.surface: A reluctant sucker eats a bit of eel and finds it revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: Unagi is the Japanese word for freshwater eel, served in sushi; FOOL loses one of its middle Os and then takes in the U.
explanation.definitionFit: Foul describes something offensive to the senses, such as a vile smell, the same as disgusting.

clue.text: Unwilling to cut length of curse

indicators.note: cutting removes a piece, so one letter is taken away

blocks.note: loath means reluctant or unwilling
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: Someone reluctant to shorten a long curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Length of curse' reads as one phrase, how long a curse is; in fact L is cut and 'of' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath can be a swear word or profanity, so it is a curse in the sense of bad language.

clue.text: Sound reasoning of the Italian soldier convincing at first

indicators.note: at first means at the beginning, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: lo is one of the Italian words for the
a GI is an American soldier
first letter of convincing

explanation.surface: An Italian soldier's arguments are persuasive from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: IL is the familiar Italian article, but LO is the form used before some consonants, and it is the one needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is the science of valid argument, so it means reasoning that holds together.

clue.text: Work on oddly dismissed retro musical about secret agent in the US

indicators.note: dismissing the odd letters sends them away, so only the even ones remain
turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
second and fourth letters of retro
Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Perón

explanation.surface: Someone works on a retro musical about a spy, then sacks people for odd behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retro' looks like the reversal signal for the musical, but its even letters supply ER, and 'about' does the reversing.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage an operative is a spy or intelligence agent, as with a CIA operative.

clue.text: Bottom overwhelmed by suffering when most hairy

indicators.note: something overwhelmed is engulfed or swamped, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: cost is loss or suffering, as in to your cost
arse is British slang for the bottom

explanation.surface: A sore behind gets most painful when it is hairiest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' looks like a position, the lowest part, but it is the backside, ARSE in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse hair is thick and rough, so the coarsest is the roughest or bristliest, a loose sense of hairy.

clue.text: That man succeeded in Wyoming with a capricious idea

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: him refers to that man
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees
WY is the postal code for Wyoming

explanation.surface: A man who did well in Wyoming on the strength of a passing fancy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeeded' reads as made it, but it is the genealogical S; HIM and S both go inside the state's code.
explanation.definitionFit: A whimsy is a fanciful or playful notion, a sudden whim, so it is an impulsive fancy.
